subject: Career
title: Negotiation Communication: Interest vs. Position
description: One-minute skill: Negotiation Communication: Interest vs. Position.

hook.text: Two siblings fight over an orange. One wants the juice. The other wants the peel for baking. Both could win.

buildup.text: Fisher and Ury's 'Getting to Yes' introduced the concept: focus on interests, not positions.

discovery.text: Positions are what people say they want. Interests are why they want it. The why opens creative solutions.

twist.text: Most workplace negotiations are positional: 'I need this budget.' 'No.' End of discussion.

climax.text: Ask: 'Help me understand what you need this to accomplish.' The answer reveals interests you can satisfy.

punchline.text: Behind every position is an interest. Find it and you'll find the deal.

quiz.question: What's the difference between positions and interests in negotiation?
options: Positions are what people want; interests are why they want it

details.summary: Interest-based negotiation, popularized in Getting to Yes by Fisher and Ury, focuses on uncovering what each party truly needs rather than arguing fixed positions. This communication approach generates creative solutions that satisfy both sides and preserves working relationships.
details.whyItMatters: Positional bargaining creates winners and losers, damaging long-term collaboration. Interest-based communication transforms negotiations from adversarial contests into joint problem-solving.
takeaways: Ask 'why' behind every stated position to uncover true interests
Generate multiple options before committing to any single solution
Use objective criteria to evaluate options fairly for both sides

faq.question: How do I uncover someone's interests when they only state positions?
faq.answer: Ask open-ended questions like 'What is most important to you about this outcome?' and 'What would an ideal solution look like for you?' Listen for emotional emphasis and underlying needs. Repeated probing usually reveals interests the other party may not have articulated even to themselves.

faq.question: Can interest-based negotiation work when the other side is adversarial?
faq.answer: Yes, though it requires more patience. Continue asking about interests even when the other side argues positions. Model the behavior you want to see. Most adversarial negotiators soften when they realize you genuinely want to find a mutually beneficial outcome.
